headline: Massachusetts offers schools $1.75 million for online-safety lessons
dek: The new grant program will help districts teach students about cyberbullying, privacy, misinformation and AI-generated content while lawmakers remain divided over broader social-media rules.
body: Massachusetts is putting $1.75 million behind a school-based response to the problems young people face online, with grants designed to teach students how to use social media more safely and responsibly. Gov. Maura Healey announced the program Wednesday during a visit to Peabody Veterans Memorial High School, where she met with students, teachers and school leaders to discuss social media, mental health and concentration in school, according to the [Massachusetts Executive Office of Education](https://www.mass.gov/news/governor-healey-announces-175-million-to-promote-safe-social-media-use-and-support-student-mental-health).

The money will flow through the new Safe, Healthy and Responsible Digital Life Grant Program, administered by the Department of Elementary and Secondary Education. Public school districts, charter public schools and educational collaboratives may apply for roughly 25 to 30 awards of up to $60,000 each. The state says funded programs can serve elementary, middle and high school students and must be carried out during the 2026–2027 school year. Applications are due Nov. 9 at 5 p.m., giving districts a short window to design programs, identify partners and explain how the work will reach students and families.

The proposed uses are broader than a one-time assembly about screen time. The administration says schools may pay for age-appropriate classroom instruction, educational materials, educator training and resources for families. Students could be taught to recognize false or misleading information, including material generated by artificial-intelligence systems; protect personal information; understand the risks of social media and cyberbullying; and make more responsible decisions online. That combination places digital literacy and student well-being in the same program rather than treating online safety only as a discipline or technology issue.

The grant pool is part of a larger $2 million fiscal 2027 investment in online safety and education. The state says $250,000 will support review of instructional materials and the development of educational videos and other resources that schools can use to teach healthy social-media habits and digital literacy. The announcement does not promise funding for every district or identify the eventual recipients. Final awards and local program designs will determine how widely the effort reaches.

Peabody gives the announcement a concrete local setting. Superintendent Josh Vadala told the state that the district has seen the effects of social media use on adolescent mental health and cyberbullying, while the state described the event as a roundtable rather than a rollout of a required statewide curriculum. The distinction matters for families: this funding creates an opportunity for districts to add instruction and support, but it does not establish one identical lesson plan or one uniform school policy for all Massachusetts students.

The grants also arrive while Beacon Hill is still debating whether to regulate the platforms themselves. [CommonWealth Beacon, reporting for the State House News Service](https://commonwealthbeacon.org/education/state-grants-schools-1-75m-to-teach-healthy-social-media-use/), said a House bill passed in April would bar children under 14 from using social-media platforms and require parental consent for 14- and 15-year-olds. A separate Senate proposal passed in July would require default settings for minors that disable or limit features such as addictive feeds, autoplay, infinite scrolling and overnight notifications. Those are legislative proposals, not rules created by Wednesday’s grant announcement.

Healey’s administration has pursued both approaches: education and platform restrictions. The governor previously proposed age-assurance requirements, stronger default privacy settings and limits on addictive features and notifications, according to the state release. Massachusetts has also opened a separate $1 million grant program to help schools become cellphone-free during the school day. The overlapping initiatives show the state is trying to address classroom distraction, online harms and mental-health concerns through several programs while the larger policy debate remains unresolved.

For districts, the immediate next step is the grant application rather than a change in student rules. Eligible applicants will need to decide which grades and communities to serve, how to involve educators and families, and how to teach students to evaluate AI-generated or misleading material without treating every online interaction as harmful. The state’s November deadline will produce the first test of whether the available money can be converted into sustained classroom practice. For families, the announcement signals new local programming may appear next school year, but the details will depend on which districts apply and which proposals DESE approves.
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: Massachusetts schools can seek $1.75M online-safety grants
seoDescription: Massachusetts opened $1.75 million in grants for schools to teach online safety, cyberbullying prevention, privacy, misinformation and AI literacy.
